title: The History of the Internet: From ARPANET to 5G
subtitle: How the network born in the US transformed the lives of Brazilians
excerpt: From ARPANET to the fifth mobile generation, discover the trajectory of the internet and its impact on the economy, education, and digital citizenship in Brazil.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The internet, which today moves billions of messages, purchases, and services, has its origins in a US military project from the 1960s. What started as ARPANET, a computer network for sharing academic resources, evolved over six decades to 5G, the fifth generation of mobile communication that is already being implemented in Brazilian cities. Understanding this trajectory helps recognize the role of innovation in the economy, education, and digital citizenship of the country.

The Origins: ARPANET and the Vision of a Connected World

In 1969, the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) of the US Department of Defense created ARPANET, connecting four universities. The goal was to ensure the exchange of information even if part of the network was destroyed, a concept of redundancy that became the basis of network architecture. The first message sent — "LO" (an attempt to type "LOGIN") — was marked as the starting point of a revolution that would surpass military borders.

From TCP/IP Protocol to Global Internet

In the 1970s, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn developed the TCP/IP protocol, which standardized the way computers exchanged data packets. In 1983, ARPANET officially adopted TCP/IP, and simultaneously, the IP addressing system became the universal standard. This change allowed different networks to interconnect, creating the network of networks we know today.

The Commercial Explosion in the 1990s

With the opening of the network for non-military use, the first commercial connections emerged. The development of the World Wide Web by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 brought to the public a graphical interface based on hypertext, making navigation accessible to laypeople. In the United States, providers like AOL and Prodigy popularized home access; in Brazil, Embratel launched the first international connection in 1991, allowing Brazilian companies to start using email and file transfer.

The Era of Browsers and the Democratization of Information

The launch of Mosaic in 1993 and, soon after, Netscape Navigator, transformed the online experience by introducing integrated images and click navigation. Brazil quickly followed: in 1995, the first commercial access provider, Geeks, began offering dial-up plans. The popularization of browsers brought to light the need for more robust infrastructure, driving the expansion of fiber optic lines in major metropolitan regions.

Mobility and the 3G and 4G Generations

The transition to mobile telephony began with 2G in the 1990s, but it was the arrival of 3G in the mid-2000s that allowed video transmission and the use of social network applications. The 4G, consolidated in Brazil from 2014, raised download speeds to dozens of megabits per second, enabling services like high-definition streaming, video conferencing, and real-time e-commerce. This evolution prepared the ground for the fifth generation.

5G: The Fifth Generation Already in Brazil

The 5G, internationally standardized in 2018, offers latency of a few milliseconds, the ability to connect millions of devices simultaneously, and rates that exceed gigabits per second in urban areas. In Brazil, the first cities to receive commercial service were major centers like São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Brasília, starting in 2022. Operators have been investing in small cell antennas to ensure densely populated coverage.

Practical Implications for the Brazilian Reader

  • Education: 5G enables live classes in augmented reality, reducing the need for travel and expanding access to quality content in remote areas.
  • Health: Telemedicine with high-resolution exam transmission can be done in real-time, improving early diagnosis.
  • Business: Small businesses can adopt cloud management systems and industrial automation without needing large investments in physical infrastructure.
  • Digital Citizenship: The increased speed and ability to connect more devices facilitate participation in online government processes, such as public consultations and service attendance.

Challenges and Future Perspectives

Despite the advances, the implementation of 5G still faces challenges of coverage in inland regions and spectrum regulation. The Brazilian government has been seeking frequency auctions that encourage private investment, while following security and privacy norms. Looking ahead, the combination of 5G with emerging technologies — such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), and cloud computing — promises to further transform the way Brazilians work, study, and relate.

In summary, the journey of the internet, from the modest ARPANET to the fast 5G, demonstrates that each technological leap brings new opportunities and responsibilities. For the Brazilian reader, understanding this history is not just curiosity: it is the basis for making the most of the tools that shape contemporary society.
